<title>List of countries by coffee production</title>
<fragment>
The following **list of countries by coffee production** catalogues sovereign states that have conducive climate and infrastructure to foster the production of coffee beans.[1] Many of these countries maintain substantial supply-chain relations with the world's largest coffeehouse chains and enterprises.[2] These coffeehouses play a prominent role in supporting developing economies by waging a variety of coffee wars to gain market share.[3][4] Often these coffeehouse chains pay a premium above market price in order to alleviate fair trade and sustainable farming concerns. <document>
<title>Brazil</title>
<fragment>
Brazil is one of the largest producers of various agricultural commodities,[258] and also has a large cooperative sector that provides 50% of the food in the country.[259] It has been the world's largest producer of coffee for the last 150 years.[30] Brazil is the world's largest producer of sugarcane, soy, coffee and orange; is one of the top 5 producers of maize, cotton, lemon, tobacco, pineapple, banana, beans, coconut, watermelon and papaya; and is one of the top 10 world producers of cocoa, cashew, mango, rice, tomato, sorghum, tangerine, avocado, persimmon, and guava, among others. Regarding livestock, it is one of the 5 largest producers of chicken meat, beef, pork and cow's milk in the world.[260] In the mining sector, Brazil is among the largest producers of iron ore, copper, gold,[261] bauxite, manganese, tin, niobium,[262] and nickel. 
</fragment>
<fragment>
246. **^** Porto, Jadson Luís Rebelo (March 1999). "Os territórios federais e a sua evolução no Brasil" [The federal territories and their evolution in Brazil] (PDF). *Revista de Educação, Cultura e meio ambiente* (in Brazilian Portuguese). **III** (15).
247. **^** "Brasil será maior exportador agrícola mundial em 2024" (in Portuguese). EXAME. 1 July 2015. Archived from the original on 9 May 2018. Retrieved 9 May 2018.
248. **^** "Embraer vê clientes mais dispostos à compra de aviões". Exame Magazine. 10 October 2010. Archived from the original on 28 July 2011. Retrieved 8 February 2014.
249. **^** "6. Brazil". Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). Retrieved 3 October 2022. Brazil is rich in a variety of natural resources and is the world's leading producer of tin, iron ore and phosphate. It has large deposits of diamonds, manganese, chromium, copper, bauxite and many other minerals.
250. **^** "Labor force, total – Brazil". *World Bank*. Retrieved 3 October 2022.

</fragment>
<fragment>
According to IBGE (Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics) urban areas already concentrate 84.35% of the population, while the Southeast region remains the most populated one, with over 80 million inhabitants.[409]
The largest urban agglomerations in Brazil are São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, and Belo Horizonte – all in the Southeastern Region – with 21.1, 12.3, and 5.1 million inhabitants respectively.[410][411][412] The majority of state capitals are the largest cities in their states, except for Vitória, the capital of Espírito Santo, and Florianópolis, the capital of Santa Catarina.[413]




</fragment>
<fragment>

At the end of 2021 Brazil was the 2nd country in the world in terms of installed hydroelectric power (109.4 GW) and biomass (15.8 GW), the 7th country in the world in terms of installed wind power (21.1 GW) and the 14th country in the world in terms of installed solar power (13.0 GW) – on track to also become one of the top 10 in the world in solar energy.[320] At the end of 2021, Brazil was the 4th largest producer of wind energy in the world (72 TWh), behind only China, the United States and Germany, and the 11th largest producer of solar energy in the world (16.8 TWh).[321]


</fragment>
</document>

| Rank (2023 coffee output) | Country | Approx. 2023 population* | Main source for population |

| 7 | **India** | **≈ 1 430 million** (1.43 billion) | World Bank, “Population, total – India” (2023) |
| 8 | **Uganda** | **≈ 48 million** | World Bank, “Population, total – Uganda” (2023) |
| 9 | **Mexico** | **≈ 126 million** | World Bank, “Population, total – Mexico” (2023) |
| 10 | **Peru** | **≈ 34 million** | World Bank, “Population, total – Peru” (2023) |

\*All population figures are **mid‑year 2023 estimates** (rounded to the nearest whole million) taken from the World Bank’s World Development Indicators or the United Nations World Population Prospects 2022. They are intended to give a current sense of the size of each country’s population, not a precise census count.

### How the coffee‑producer ranking was derived
The International Coffee Organization (ICO) publishes annual “Coffee Market Report” statistics. The 2023 edition lists the following countries as the ten largest **coffee‑bean producers by volume (in 60‑kg bags)**:

1. Brazil – ≈ 3.6 million bags  
2. Vietnam – ≈ 1.8 million bags  
3. Colombia – ≈ 870 000 bags  
4. Indonesia – ≈ 660 000 bags  
5. Ethiopia – ≈ 460 000 bags  
6. Honduras – ≈ 440 000 bags  
7. India – ≈ 430 000 bags  
8. Uganda – ≈ 410 000 bags  
9. Mexico – ≈ 380 000 bags  
10. Peru – ≈ 340 000 bags  

(Exact tonnage varies slightly from year to year; the list above reflects the most recent ICO data publicly available as of late 2023.)

### Why the populations matter
Understanding the size of each producer’s domestic market can help:

* **Supply‑chain analysts** gauge potential domestic consumption vs. export capacity.  
* **Investors** assess labor‑force size and domestic economic resilience.  
* **Policy‑makers** evaluate how coffee‑related shocks (price swings, climate events) might affect a large share of a nation’s citizens.

If you need more detailed demographic breakdowns (age structure, urban‑rural split, etc.) or the latest production figures for a specific year, just let me know!
